chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
title: Chick Webb and Buddy Rich
summary: Crawford calls Chick Webb a great boss-drummer whose speed Buddy Rich copied, and says Rich and Sinatra clashed.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Okay, now let's -- see, now where -- we've got you -- we've talked about you knowing Sid Catlett, and the first time you heard him was in the early '30s.
Now, Chick Webb you liked a lot too, didn't you?
Uh-huh. Did you get to know him?
Uh-huh. What kind of a person was he?

Well, Chick was the boss of his band, and he was handicapped a certain -- he wasn't handicapped, just disfigured. He was hunchbacked, came out of Baltimore, played the Savoy. Yeah, he held forth there at the Savoy anytime he wanted to (inaudible) under Buchanan and all that, guys like that who ran the Savoy Ballroom. Oh, Chick was a great drummer.
Well, what was it about him that you liked?
His speed, his speed. He was fantastic.
Well, you know, I just recently read -- Buddy Rich said that Chick didn't have too much technique.

Yeah, but what technique he did have Buddy Rich copied, tried to copy and steal it. Buddy didn't like nobody but himself. He and Frank Sinatra used to get into more battles. Oh, yeah, that -- until Buddy Rich started taking up Karate. Frank studied it too. Oh, they used to -- when they were with Tommy Dorsey's band, they couldn't get
along for nothing, Frank and Buddy Rich.
Buddy Rich only liked himself. That's a fact.
